title: The tulip crash that ruined Holland is mostly a story.
description:
The tulip crash that ruined Holland is mostly a story. Historian Anne Goldgar found little evidence of widespread financial ruin.

Wrote that substantial merchants were reduced almost to beggary, drawing partly on satirical Dutch poems and pamphlets.

Far fewer people took part than the legend says. Goldgar counted about 285 traders in Haarlem, 60 in Amsterdam and 25 in Enkhuizen, and says those are underestimates.

What 1,100 guilders for a Switsers bulb equalled in a master carpenter's wages. Rich merchants could afford it.

She found virtually no bankruptcies traced to tulips. Bankruptcy records are patchy, so this is a lack of evidence, not proof.

The real damage was to trust, in a society that ran on credit.

Sources:
- https://www.history.com/news/tulip-mania-financial-crash-holland - History.com; established that Charles Mackay's 1841 account is the source of the ruin story, that he drew on satirical Dutch poems and pamphlets, and that Anne Goldgar's archival work found little evidence of wider economic damage.
- https://www.historytoday.com/print/pdf/node/54516/debug - History Today, Goldgar's own article; established about 285 traders in Haarlem, 60 in Amsterdam and 25 in Enkhuizen (underestimates), that 1,100 guilders for Switsers bulbs was about three years' wages for a master carpenter yet affordable to rich merchants, that she found virtually no bankruptcies caused by tulips though records are patchy, and that the real disruption was a breach of trust in a credit based society.
